locus: Boym, Cafraria (1644), para. 'Omnes Cafres sunt nigri coloris'
question: Tu vero quoties homines comedisti?
answer: Bis, semel caput unius, altera vice pedes alterius.
derivation: Direct-speech exchange. The narrator (author) asks the Cafer how many times he has eaten men; the Cafer answers in direct speech. Dropped the framing speech tag 'inquit' interleaved in the reply ('"Bis", inquit, "semel caput unius..."'). Question kept verbatim; answer is the contiguous utterance with internal 'inquit' removed. Stops at the full stop ending the reply.

locus: Boym, Cafraria (1644), para. 'Quando Cafres salutant aliquem'
question: Quid melius, panisne, oryza an milium?
answer: Panis implet ventrem et transit, similiter oryza; solum milium implet et manet.
derivation: Direct-speech exchange introduced by the framing participle 'Quaesiti' (dropped as narration of the asking) and the speech verb 'respondent' (dropped). The verbatim interrogative 'quid melius, panisne, oryza an milium' is the question; the quoted reply is the answer, kept verbatim and contiguous. First-word capitalization and terminal punctuation normalized; the parenthetical aside that follows the quotation ('carnem tamen libenter comedunt...') is outside the answer and omitted.

question: Ubi es?
answer: Hic, hic, hic!
derivation: Search party calls out 'Ubi es?' and the severed head answers, locating itself. Framing dropped: 'ad voces se invicem cohortantium et utpote socii ad socium alternatim clamantium' before the question, and 'illud respondebat designando locum patria lingua dicens' before the answer. The head's literal utterance is 'Her, her, her!' in the vernacular; the author supplies its Latin equivalent ('quod interpretatum Latinus sermo exprimit'), so the answer is given as the Latin words 'Hic, hic, hic!'. Stopped before the following narration 'Nec umquam eadem repetendo clamare destitit...'.

locus: Abelard, Dialogus inter Philosophum, Iudaeum et Christianum (Philosophus-Christianus exchange on the way to the highest good)
question: Et quam, rogo, viam ad hoc summum bonum, id est virtutem, perveniendi constituebant?
answer: Ipsum prorecto moralis lectionis studium vel domandae carnis exercitium, ut bona in habitum solidata voluntas virtus dici queat.
derivation: Christianus asks a real interrogative (quam viam... constituebant?), and the Philosophus answers directly. Dropped the speaker labels 'Christianus:' and 'Philosophus:' as drama/dialogue scaffolding. The answer is a single sentence to its first full stop; nothing was trimmed from it. Question quoted verbatim including the speaker's own interjection 'rogo'.

locus: Abelard, Dialogus inter Philosophum, Iudaeum et Christianum (Philosophus-Christianus exchange defining the blessed man)
question: Et quem esse beatum definiunt?
answer: Beatum quasi bene aptum dicunt, hoc est in omnibus bene et facile se agentem, ut idem sit scilicet beatum esse, quod bonis moribus, id est virtutibus, pollere.
derivation: Christianus poses a genuine interrogative (quem... beatum definiunt?) and the Philosophus answers it directly with a definition. Dropped the 'Christianus:' and 'Philosophus:' speaker labels. The answer is one contiguous sentence to its full stop; nothing omitted internally.

question: Cur post conversionem nostram, quam tu solus facere decrevisti, in tantam tibi negligentiam atque oblivionem venerim ut nec colloquio presentis recreer nec absentis epistola consoler?
answer: Concupiscentia te mihi potius quam amicitia sociavit, libidinis ardor potius quam amor.
derivation: Heloise poses and answers her own question. Cut the framing imperative 'Dic unum, si vales,' before the question (a speech-tag urging him to tell). After the question, cut the meta-narration of the answering 'dic, inquam, si vales, aut ego quod sentio immo quod omnes suspicantur dicam.' before the answer. The answer is taken to its first full stop; what follows ('Ubi igitur quod desiderabas cessavit...') elaborates rather than directly answering the 'cur'. Capitalized 'Cur', added terminal '?'.

question: Quis tamen ille novus perstringit lumina fulgor? Quam mitra effigiem distinxit pictor, honesto surgentem e tumulo, alatoque satellite fultam?
answer: Agnosco faciem, vultu latet alter in illo Wainfletus.
derivation: The poet poses a rhetorical double question about a bright figure in the painting ('Who is this new brightness? What figure...?') and answers it himself by identifying the face as Wainflete. Answer ends at the first full stop after 'Wainfletus'; what follows ('sic ille oculos, sic ora ferebat: Eheu quando animi par invenietur imago?') is descriptive elaboration turning into a separate unanswered lament, so it is cut. No framing/narration to strip; first-word capitalization and terminal '?' normalized.

question: Nonne satis tibi est hinc quod ait Tullius: amicitia est rerum humanarum et divinarum cum benevolentia et caritate consensio?
answer: Si tibi sufficit ista diffinitio, mihi iudico satisfactum esse.
derivation: Stripped speaker labels 'Aelredus.' (before the question) and 'Ivo.' (before the answer), the title lines, the CAPUT headers, and the trailing Latin-Library footer. Aelred asks (real interrogative, 'Nonne...?') whether Tullius's quoted definition suffices; Ivo answers affirmatively that he is satisfied. Answer is its single full sentence; nothing cut.

question: Quid est igitur quod inter amicissimos graves ortas inimicitias legimus?
answer: Haec volo interim credas numquam fuisse amicum, qui laedere potuit eum quem in amicitia semel recepit; sed nec eum verae amicitiae gustasse delicias qui vel laesus desiit diligere quem semel amavit.
derivation: Stripped speaker labels 'Ivo.'/'Aelredus.'. Ivo asks (interrogative 'Quid est... quod') how enmities can arise among the closest of friends. Aelred's reply opens with a non-answering deflection, 'De his suo loco uberius, si Deus voluerit, disputabimus.' ('we will discuss this at length elsewhere'); the answer start is advanced past it to the operative answering sentence, which explains that such people were never true friends. Window ends at the first full stop, before 'Omni enim tempore diligit qui amicus est.'

question: Nonne sapientia multi abutuntur, qui ex ea hominibus placere cupiunt, vel in seipsis pro collata sibi sapientia superbiunt; vel certe hi qui eam venalem habent, et quaestum estimant pietatem?
answer: Hinc tibi satisfaciet noster Augustinus, cuius verba sunt haec: qui sibi placet, stulto homini placet; quia profecto stultus est, qui sibi placet.
derivation: Stripped speaker labels 'Ivo.'/'Aelredus.' and dropped the asking-framing interjection 'quaeso te' ('I ask you') from inside the question, leaving the speaker's own words in source order. Real interrogative ('Nonne... abutuntur?') asking whether wisdom is abused; Aelred answers by citing Augustine that whoever abuses wisdom does not in fact have it. Answer ends at the first full stop, before 'Qui vero stultus est, sapiens non est...'.

question: Quid si pessimi quique vel ethnici in consensu facinorum et flagitiorum sic se diligant, ut velint pro invicem mori, eos ne ad summam amicitiae conscendisse fatebimur?
answer: Absit; cum inter pessimos amicitia esse non possit.
derivation: Stripped speaker labels 'Galterus.'/'Aelredus.'. Galter asks (interrogative '...eos ne... fatebimur?') whether the wicked who would die for one another have reached the summit of friendship; Aelred answers no, since friendship cannot exist among the wicked. Whole reply kept; nothing cut.

question: Quid igitur nobis cum amicitia, qui boni non sumus?
answer: Ego bonum non ita ad vivum reseco, ut quidam qui neminem volunt esse bonum, nisi eum cui ad perfectionem nihil desit.
derivation: Stripped speaker labels 'Galterus.'/'Aelredus.'. Galter asks (interrogative 'Quid... nobis cum amicitia') what they have to do with friendship since they are not good; Aelred answers by redefining 'good' more loosely, so that they qualify. Window ends at the first full stop, before 'Nos hominem bonum dicimus, qui...'.

question: Si prospera nostra nulla umquam adversitas interpolet, quomodo amici probabitur fides?
answer: Multa sunt alia quibus probatur fides amici, quamuis in sinistris maxime.
derivation: Stripped speaker labels 'Gratianus.'/'Aelredus.'. Gratian asks (interrogative 'quomodo... probabitur fides') how a friend's faith is tested if no adversity ever interrupts prosperity; Aelred answers that there are many other ways it is proved, though most of all in misfortune. Answer is its single full sentence; the following sentence ('Nam ut superius diximus...') is left out.

locus: Vita Sororis Agnetis, De transitu eius (cap. 11)
question: Heu me, mater karissima, vt quid filias tuas & me specialiter uis derelinquere! Et quis me miseram consolabitur te, uirgo dulcissima, moriente?
answer: Ne fleueris, Katherina, quia in breui recipies consolacionem a domino!
derivation: The dying Agnes is approached by the ailing sister Katherina Erhardi, whose plea contains genuine interrogatives ('vt quid... uis derelinquere', 'quis me miseram consolabitur'). The entire utterance is quoted verbatim and contiguous as the question. Framing dropped before the question: 'uerbaque doloris ingeminans dicebat.' Agnes's reply is quoted in full as the answer; it genuinely answers the 'who will console me' question with 'you will receive consolation from the Lord.' Framing dropped before the answer: 'At uirgo Cristi miseria mota super eam dixit,'. Stopped before the following narration 'Et cum infirma, una cum aliis sororibus instantissime postularet...'. No editorial brackets in either span. Other question-marked exchanges were rejected: the resuscitated soul's 'Cur me reuocas...?' (line 51) receives only an action, not a verbal answer; in the queen's dream-vision (line 113) 'Numquid dormis?'/'non' is trivial and not self-contained, 'Numquid est hic... auia mea sancta Agnes?' is answered only by narration ('sorore hoc affirmante'), and 'Cur pro te orabo?' is answered by a plea/retort rather than a real answer.

locus: Alanus de Insulis, De planctu Naturae, quaestio 1 et solutio
question: Tu viae causam resera petenti, cur petis terras, peregrina coelis? Cur tuae nostris deitatis offers munera terris?
answer: Cum omnia lege suae originis meis legibus teneantur obnoxia, mihique debeant jus statuti vectigalis persolvere, fere omnia tributarii juris exhibitione legitima, meis edictis regulariter obsequuntur; sed ab hujus universitatis regula, solus homo anomala exceptione excluditur, qui pudoris trabea denudatus, impudicitiaeque meretricali prostibulo prostitutus, in suae dominae majestatem, litis audet excitare tumultum, imo etiam in matrem intestini belli rabiem inflammare.
derivation: Alanus's first quaestio (verse) asks why Natura, a stranger from heaven, descends to earth; I kept his full interrogative including the imperative setup 'Tu viae causam resera petenti' so the cur-clauses have their frame. I skipped the non-answering preamble 'Ratio naturae' (a counter-question 'An ignoras...' plus a condition) and started the answer at the 'Solutio primae quaestionis': Natura's operative reply that all things obey her laws but man alone is the lawless exception who incites strife against her. Answer ends at the first full stop ('...rabiem inflammare.'); what follows ('Caetera quibus meae gratiae...') elaborates with further examples.

locus: Alanus de Insulis, De planctu Naturae, quaestio 2 et solutio
question: Ora cur fletus pluvia rigantur? Quid tui vultus lacrymae prophetant?
answer: Ideo enim a supernis coelestis regiae secretariis egrediens, ad hujus caducae terrenitatis occasum deveni, ut de exsecrabilibus hominum excessibus, tecum quasi cum familiari et secretario meo, querimoniale lamentum exponerem, tecumque decernerem, tali criminum oppositioni, qualis poenae debeat dari responsio: ut praedictorum facinorum morsibus coaequata punitio, poenae talionem remordeat.
derivation: Alanus's second quaestio (verse) asks why her cheeks run with weeping and what her tears foretell; I quoted the two genuine interrogative lines, omitting the following declarative gloss 'Fletus interni satis est doloris lingua fidelis' (not a question). The 'Solutio secundae quaestionis' answers directly: she descended to lay out a lamenting complaint about men's crimes and to decide their punishment. Answer is one sentence to its first full stop ('...poenae talionem remordeat.'); what follows ('Tunc ego: O rerum omnium mediatrix...') is Alanus's transition to the next question.

locus: Alanus de Insulis, De planctu Naturae, quaestio 3 et responsio
question: Miror cur poetarum commenta pertractans, solummodo in humani generis pestes, praedictarum invectionum armas aculeos, cum et eodem exorbitationis pede, deos claudicasse legamus?
answer: Quamvis ergo, ut poetae testati sunt plerique homines talibus Veneris terminis sint abusi ad litteram, narratio tamen illa vel deos esse, vel ipsos in Veneris gymnasiis latuisse, mentitur, et in nimiae falsitatis vesperascit occasum: ideo, ista nube taciturnitatis obduxi, alia vero in luce verae narrationis explicui.
derivation: Alanus's third quaestio asks why she attacks only mankind's sins and not the gods, who (per the poets) sinned likewise; I stripped the speech tag 'Tunc ego:' and kept the interrogative sentence, omitting the following declarative examples (Jupiter/Ganymede, Bacchus, Apollo) that merely illustrate it. The 'Responsio naturae' opens with a long non-answering preamble of rhetorical counter-questions and a disquisition on poetic fiction; I advanced the answer's start to its operative answering sentence, which directly resolves the premise: the tale that gods exist or hid in Venus's games is a lie, so she covered it in silence. Answer ends at the full stop ('...verae narrationis explicui.'); what follows is Alanus conceding and moving on.

locus: Alanus de Insulis, De planctu Naturae, quaestio 4 et solutio
question: Miror, cur quaedam tuae tunicae portiones, quae texturae matrimonii deberent esse confines, in ea parte suae conjunctionis patiantur divortia, in qua hominis imaginem picturae repraesentant insomnia?
answer: Jam ex explicatis potes elicere, quid mysticum figuret scissurae figurata parenthesis: cum enim ut diximus, plerique homines in suam matrem vitiorum armentur injuriis, inde inter se et ipsam maximum chaos dissensionis firmantes, in me violentas manus violenter injiciunt, mea sibi particulatim vestimenta diripiunt, et quam reverentiae deberent honore vestire, me vestibus orphanatam (quantum in ipsis est) cogunt meretricaliter lupari; hoc ergo in tegumento per hanc scissuram depingitur, quod in solius hominis vitiosis insultibus, mea pudoris ornamenta scissionis contumelias patiuntur.
derivation: Alanus's fourth quaestio asks why parts of Natura's tunic are torn precisely where the picture depicts the image of man; I stripped the speech tag 'Tunc ego' and capitalized 'Miror'. The 'Solutio quaestionis' answers directly: the tear depicts that man alone, arming himself against his mother Nature with vices, tears at her ornaments. The whole reply is a single sentence (colons/semicolons internal) ending at the first full stop ('...scissionis contumelias patiuntur.'); the round-bracket '(quantum in ipsis est)' is the author's own parenthesis, not an editorial angle-bracket supplement, so it is retained. What follows ('Tunc ego: Jam mearum dubitationum fluctus...') is Alanus's transition.

question: Cur quaeris tibi concessum? Cur poscis inepte quod Natura parat, quod mors uicina minatur?
answer: Vtere quae restat uita nec quaere propinquos anticipare dies.
derivation: Within the iuuenis's single speech to Senectus (verse poem; stripped the speech tag 'Prodit in hec:' and the [149-209] line-number marker). The speaker poses real interrogatives ('Why do you seek for yourself what is granted? Why foolishly ask for what Nature is preparing, what nearby death threatens?') and answers them himself. Question: I take the two contiguous 'Cur...' interrogative sentences; I omit the preceding 'Cur fata paras... cui uiuere fatum?' line to keep the question tight on the operative 'why seek death' point. Answer: the operative imperative 'Vtere quae restat uita nec quaere propinquos anticipare dies' (ends at the semicolon/first full sense stop); I cut the trailing maxim 'uite compendia mortem solentur, mortis dispendia uita repenset' which elaborates rather than answers.

question: Vincere cur uictos temptas? Cur bella mouere quaeris in imbelles?
answer: Satis est potuisse nec ultra nobilitas animi querit, nisi uincere posse.
derivation: Within Fraus's flattering speech to the iuuenis (verse poem; stripped the [307-353] line-number marker and the narration 'Has ergo mouet illa preces... palliat artem:'). Fraus poses real interrogatives ('Why do you try to conquer the conquered? Why seek to wage war on the unwarlike?') and answers them herself in the same breath ('It is enough to have been able, and nobility of spirit seeks nothing beyond, except being able to win'). Question: the two contiguous 'cur...' interrogative sentences. Answer: the resolving statement immediately following, to its full stop (the speech ends there).

locus: Albertanus, Ars loquendi et tacendi, Quis, punctum secundum
question: Cur tantum taceret, an quia stultus esset?
answer: Stultus tacere non potest.
derivation: From 'Nam et quidam sapiens interrogatus, cur tantum taceret, an quia stultus esset, respondit: Stultus tacere non potest.' Dropped the speech-tag framing 'Nam et quidam sapiens interrogatus' and 'respondit'; the indirect question 'cur tantum taceret, an quia stultus esset' is the verbatim content of what was asked, normalized with a terminal '?'. Answer is the full responding utterance to the first stop; what follows ('Alibi Salomo dixit...') is a new citation.

locus: Albertanus, Ars loquendi et tacendi, Quis, punctum quartum
question: Quomodo optime posset dicere?
answer: Si tantummodo dixeris quod bene scieris.
derivation: From 'Nam quidam sapiens interrogatus, quomodo optime posset dicere, respondit: Si tantummodo dixeris quod bene scieris.' Dropped framing 'Nam quidam sapiens interrogatus' and 'respondit'; 'quomodo optime posset dicere' is the verbatim asked content, normalized with '?'. Answer ends at the first full stop; what follows ('Et Jesus Sidrach: Si est tibi intellectus...') is a new citation.

locus: Albertanus, Ars loquendi et tacendi, Quid, punctum octavum (Ps. 119:3)
question: Quid detur aut quid apponatur ad linguam dolosam?
answer: Dabuntur acutae sagittae potentis Dei cum carbonibus desolatoriis.
derivation: From 'Et idem praeclare quaerit: Quid detur aut quid apponatur ad linguam dolosam? Et respondet verbo terribili: «Dabuntur acutae sagittae potentis Dei cum carbonibus desolatoriis.»' Dropped the framing 'Et idem praeclare quaerit' and 'Et respondet verbo terribili' and the surrounding quotation guillemets; the prophet poses the question and answers it himself. Answer is the full responding utterance; what follows ('Cavendum tibi summe...') is new exposition.

locus: Albertanus, Liber Consolationis et Consilii, Caput XXXIV-XXXV (De munitione)
question: Quomodo domum meam aliter munire valeam?
answer: Munitio multiplex est.
derivation: Melibeus's direct interrogative; stripped the speech tag 'At Melibeus respondens dixit:'. Stripped the intervening scaffolding 'Prudentia respondit dicens:' and the chapter heading 'Caput XXXV. De munitione.' Took Prudentia's first answering sentence 'Munitio multiplex est.' as the operative reply ('fortification is manifold'); cut before the elaboration 'Est enim munitio, quae ad dilectionem pertinet...' which begins enumerating kinds with an embedded Tullius quotation.

locus: Albertanus, Liber Consolationis et Consilii, Caput XLVIII (De guerra vitanda per reconciliationem)
question: Quomodo possum reconciliari meis inimicis? quia ipsi initium discordiae fecerunt, nec reconciliationem quaerunt.
answer: Si adversarii tui, te velle reconciliationem, crederent, cum magna devotione illam a te postularent.
derivation: Melibeus's direct interrogative; stripped the speech tag 'At Melibeus dixit:'. Kept the contiguous 'quia ipsi...quaerunt' clause as setup for the question. Stripped 'Prudentia vero respondit:' and took her first sentence as the answer; cut before 'Audivi namque, quod de peccato...' which then digresses into supporting authorities (Prophet, Apostle, Seneca) on pursuing peace.

question: Si ergo, dum pauper clamat, Deus clamare intelligitur et nos non exaudiemus eum clamantem, quare ipse nos clamantes exaudire deberet?
answer: Certe ipse rationabilter non debet nos exaudire nisi de misericordia sua hoc faciat.
derivation: Authorial rhetorical question and its self-answer in the De auditu section. The conditional setup 'Si ergo, dum pauper clamat... clamantem' is kept verbatim so that 'ipse' (God) and 'nos clamantes' have referents. The answer is the immediately following sentence, which directly responds to the 'quare... deberet?' question; the text then moves to the next section (De gustu). Scaffolding (title line, rule separators, footer) is outside this span and not included.

locus: Albertanus of Brescia, Sermo 3 (on Iob 6:30, the word "vere")
question: Quid est veritas?
answer: Certe Deus veritas est.
derivation: The preacher poses the question himself and answers it. Question is the second occurrence of 'Quid est veritas?' (the first, before Pilate, is explicitly left unanswered: 'Noluit respondere'). Answer ends at the first full stop, before the supporting scriptural citation 'ut ipse dicit in Evangelio: "Ego sum via, veritas, et vita."'

question: Vidisti hominem velocem ad loquendum?
answer: Stulticia magis speranda est, quam illius corectio.
derivation: Quoted Solomonic proverb posing a rhetorical question that it then answers. The framing 'Et Salomon ait:' is dropped. Answer is the full continuation of the proverb; stops at the full stop before the next citation 'Et alibi: "Qui prius respondit..."'.

locus: Albertanus of Brescia, Sermo 3 (on the word "iudicate")
question: Numquid ergo erit contrarium verbum Domini dicto Prophete?
answer: Absit, si ea attenderitis, que sunt in iudicio necessaria.
derivation: The preacher raises the apparent contradiction between the Prophet's 'recte iudicate' and the Lord's 'Nolite iudicare', then answers his own question. Answer ends at the first full stop, before the enumeration 'et certe, meo arbitrio, septem sunt in iudicio...' that elaborates.

locus: Albertanus of Brescia, Sermo 3 (woman caught in adultery, cf. John 8:10-11)
question: Mulier, ubi sunt qui te accusant?
answer: Nemo, Domine.
derivation: Direct-speech exchange. The Lord's question 'Mulier, ubi sunt qui te accusant?' is answered by the woman: framing 'Et illa dixit:' is dropped, leaving 'Nemo, Domine.' The Lord's following 'Si nullus te accusat...' is a further pronouncement, not the answer to this question.

question: Si ingenuam es, quomodo ancillam Christi te esse comemoras?
answer: Summa ingenuita hec est in qua servitus, Christi comemoratur.
derivation: Quintianus rebukes Agatha and asks a direct interrogative (quomodo...?); Agatha answers directly. Cut the framing tag 'Et cum ille reprehendisset eam, dicens:' before the question and 'et illa respondit:' before the answer. After the answer follows the citation tag 'ut in passione dicte Virginis legitur', which is omitted. Capitalization of 'si' normalized to 'Si'.

locus: Albertanus, De amore, Liber III, Caput XV (John 8:10-11)
question: Mulier, ubi sunt qui te accusant?
answer: Nemo, Domine.
derivation: Direct-speech exchange from the adultery pericope quoted in Caput XV. Stripped the speech tags 'dixit' (before the question) and 'Et illa dixit' (before the answer). The question is a genuine interrogative ('where are those who accuse you?'); the woman's reply 'Nemo, Domine.' answers it directly. Stopped the answer at the first full stop; the following sentence 'Et ille respondet, "Si nullus te accusat, nec ego te condempnabo."' is Jesus's subsequent verdict, not the answer to the question, so it is excluded.

locus: Albertanus, De amore et dilectione, lib. IV, cap. I (De iustitia), Seneca quote
question: Sequitur autem ratio naturam. Quid est ergo ratio?
answer: Nature imitatio.
derivation: Within the Seneca quotation the author poses a self-answered question. Setup 'Sequitur autem ratio naturam' is kept verbatim so 'ratio' has a referent; the question is the interrogative 'Quid est ergo ratio?' The answer is the immediately following two-word reply 'Nature imitatio.', stopping at its full stop before the text turns to a new definition ('Aliter eciam diffinitur...'). Dropped the surrounding framing 'de qua Seneca in epistolis dixit'.

locus: Albert of Aix, Historia Hierosolymitanae Expeditionis 1.4
question: O fidelissime Christianorum, quid super his compellas et inquietas paternitatem nostram, cum nostrae vires vel potentia non magis quam formica exigua adversus tantorum superbiam computentur? Vita enim nostra aut assiduis redimitur tributis; aut mortiferis deputatur suppliciis. Et majora asperamus de die in diem adfore pericula, nisi Christianorum adfuerint auxilia, quae tua legatione invitamus.
answer: Qua de causa, ob Domini gratiam, et vestram liberationem et sanctorum emundationem, Domino comite, vita sospite rediens imprimis dominum apostolicum requiram, deinde omnes primates Christianorum reges, duces, comites, et principatum regni tenentes, servitutis vestrae miseriam, et angustiarum tolerantiam cunctis insinuans.
derivation: The patriarch's entire speech is an extended question-plus-plea (why do you press us when we are powerless, and we beg for Christian aid), quoted verbatim and contiguous as the question after dropping the framing tag 'pia et fidelia profert responsa:'. Petrus's reply is framed by 'Cui Petrus in hunc modum respondit:' (dropped). The answer skips Petrus's non-answering preamble ('Venerande Pater, satis comperimus... oppressionibus gentilium.', an acknowledgement of the Christians' weakness) and takes the operative answering sentence in which he promises to seek the pope and the Christian princes' aid; it stops before the closing sentence 'Jam omnia inter se haec nuntia aeque videntur ut fiant.'. Section markers [0390C]/[0391A] and the colon framing were stripped.

locus: Albert of Aix, Historia Hierosolymitanae Expeditionis 2.2-2.3
question: Regi Hungarorum CALOMANO GODEFRIDUS, dux Lotharingorum, et caeteri comprimores Galliae, salutem et omne bonum in Christo. Mirantur domini et principes nostri, cum Christianae professionis sitis, cur tam crudeli martyrio exercitum Dei viventis interemistis, terram vero et regnum pertransire interdixistis, et variis calumniis eos affecistis. Quapropter nunc timore et dubietate concussi, Tollenburg moram facere decreverunt, donec ex ore regis intelligant cur tam crudele facinus a Christianis, persecutoribus Christianorum, commissum sit.
answer: Non Christianorum persecutores sumus, sed quidquid crudelitatis ostendimus aut in illorum interitu commisimus, nimia necessitate compulsi fecimus.
derivation: Whole legation of Godfrey and the Frankish princes to King Calomanus (CAP. II) is the question; it genuinely asks 'cur ... interemistis' / 'cur tam crudele facinus ... commissum sit' (why did you slaughter the army of God). Dropped the framing tag 'ut legationem tantorum principum hoc modo aperirent:' before it, the guillemets, and the stray section marker [0411C] that fell mid-speech before 'Christo'. The answer is the king's reply (CAP. III); dropped the framing 'Respondit rex, universo coetu suorum audiente:'. The poet directly asks the dead Octavius what killed him: 'What god, Octavius, took you from us? Or, as they say, the harsh cups of too much wine?' (lines 1-2). Octavius's ghost answers in quotation marks (lines 3-4): 'I drank with you, if there is blame; his own fates follow each man: what guilt do the innocent cups bear?' — directly rebutting the wine/cups hypothesis posed in the question. Stripped the surrounding quotation marks (presentation). Kept the whole quoted reply verbatim and contiguous as the answer, since its closing clause ('quid inmeriti crimen habent cyathi?') is what actually answers the 'pocula dura mero' part of the question; stopped at the end of the quotation and did not extend into 'scripta quidem tua nos multum mirabimur' (line 5), which is the poet resuming, not part of the reply.

question: Cur piscium quaedam genera quaesisti?
answer: Quasi id cognitionis gratia philosopho facere non liceat, quod luxurioso gulae causa liceret.
derivation: Quoted charge of the prosecution introduced with the speech tag 'inquit', which is dropped as framing per rule 1; the interrogative 'Cur ... quaesisti?' is a genuine question. Apuleius's reply ('Quasi ... liceret') answers it (a philosopher may seek fish for knowledge as a glutton does for his belly) and is taken to its first full stop; the next sentence (27.7) begins a new quoted charge. No interior words altered or omitted.

question: Cur mulier libera tibi nupsit post annos XIII uiduitatis?
answer: Quasi non magis mirandum sit quod tot annis non nubserit.
derivation: Verbatim quoted charge (a real 'Cur ...?' interrogative) followed immediately by Apuleius's answering retort, taken to its first full stop. The following sentence (27.8) is the next quoted charge, so the window stops there. Nothing added or reordered.

question: Cur prius, quam tibi nuberet, scripsit nescio quid in epistula quod sibi uidebatur?
answer: Quasi quisquam debeat causas alienae sententiae reddere.
derivation: Verbatim quoted 'Cur ...?' charge with Apuleius's answering retort, taken to its first full stop. The following item ('At enim maior natu non est iuuenem aspernata.') is a declarative statement, not a question, so it is excluded. Nothing added or reordered.

question: Ergo iam ille bonus filius meus habet amicam aliquam? prome agedum, quae sola mihi servis amanter, nomen eius, quae puerum ingenuum et investem sollicitavit, sive illa de Nympharum populo seu de Horarum numero seu de Musarum choro vel de mearum Gratiarum ministerio.
answer: Nescio, domina: puto puellam--si probe memini, Psyches nomine dicitur--efflicte cupere.
derivation: Direct-speech exchange between Venus and the gull. Stripped the framing tag 'at Venus irata solidum exclamat repente:' before Venus's words and normalized the initial capital. Venus's whole speech is one demand-question (does Cupid have a girlfriend, and what is her name); kept it contiguous and verbatim. The bird's reply is stripped of the interleaved framing 'Nec loquax illa conticuit avis, sed ... inquit, ...' and 'domina:' retains its place; the answer runs to its single full stop ('efflicte cupere.') and genuinely answers by naming Psyche. The '--' marks are the edition's parenthetical dashes (not editorial angle brackets) and are kept.

question: Nullone conexu natura se vinxit, sed in divinam et humanam partem partitam se et interruptam ac veluti debilem passa est?
answer: Nullus deus miscetur hominibus, sed hoc praecipuum eorum sublimitatis specimen est, quod nulla adtrectatione nostra contaminantur.
derivation: Author poses the question (preceded by the framing exclamation 'Quid igitur?', dropped) and answers it himself. The answer's framing tag 'Nam, ut idem Plato ait,' narrates the citation and is dropped; the operative answering clause 'Nullus deus miscetur hominibus...' is kept, capitalized at the new start. Window ends at the first full stop, before the sentence on stars ('Pars eorum tantummodo...') which digresses.

question: Vacabitne animalibus suis atque erit ista naturae pars mortua ac debilis?
answer: Immo enim si sedulo advertas, ipsae quoque aves per terrestre animal, non aerium rectius perhibeantur.
derivation: Author asks whether the vast air-region will be void of its own animals and dead; answers with 'Immo' rejecting that premise. Preceding framing exclamations 'Quid igitur tanta vis aeris...?' and 'Quid tandem?' are dropped as the lead-in. Editorial supplement '(per)' has its parentheses stripped, word 'per' kept. Window ends at the first full stop, before the elaboration on birds' terrestrial life ('Enim semper illis victus...').

question: Qui potest videri perfectus fuisse, qui a priore statu ad alium rectiorem statum migrat, cum praesertim nemo sponte capessat nova, nisi quem paenituit priorum?
answer: Non potest enim subsequi illa mutata ratio sine praecedentium infirmatione.
derivation: Author asks how one can seem to have been perfect who changes state; answers 'Non potest...' directly. The lead-in connective 'Porro autem' is dropped and the relative 'qui' capitalized at the new start. The answer is its own complete sentence ending at the full stop; the following sentence ('Quapropter debet deus...') draws the consequence and is excluded.

question: Non illi norunt arvum colere vel aurum colare vel equum domare vel taurum subigere vel ovem vel capram tondere vel pascere. Quid igitur est?
answer: Unum pro his omnibus norunt: sapientiam percolunt tam magistri senes quam discipuli iuniores.
derivation: Authorial self-posed question about the gymnosophistae. Kept the preceding 'Non illi norunt arvum colere...vel pascere.' verbatim as setup so 'Quid igitur est?' has a referent (what they do, given the listed crafts they do not practice). Answer is the contiguous reply through the first full stop; the colon before 'sapientiam' is not a sentence end, so the window extends to 'iuniores.' What follows the cut is 'Nec quicquam aeque penes illos laudo...', which digresses, so it is excluded.

question: Quid faciam?
answer: Cupio gratus videri, sed prae gaudio nondum mihi vacat gratias agere.
derivation: Author poses 'Quid faciam?' and answers it himself in the next sentence. Answer taken to the first full stop ('gratias agere.'). What follows ('Nemo me, nemo ex illis tristioribus velit in isto vituperare...') turns to a new point and is excluded.

question: Quid enim mundo praestantius?
answer: Lauda, quam putas, speciem: portio a te laudabitur mundi; admirare, quam voles, temperantiam, ordinationem, figuram: hic et per hunc illud quodcumque est invenietur esse laudandum.
derivation: Authorial rhetorical question opening section XXII, immediately answered by the author himself: whatever you praise turns out to be a portion of, or praiseworthy through, the world. The section marker 'XXII.' was stripped. The answer runs to the first full stop (after 'esse laudandum'); the interior colons are not sentence-ends per the guidance, so they are retained within the single answering sentence. The next sentence ('Nam quid, oro te, ornatum...') begins a fresh rhetorical move and is not included.

question: Potens illa et regina caupona quid mulieris est?
answer: Saga et divina, potens caelum deponere, terram suspendere, fontes durare, montes diluere, manes sublimare, deos infimare, sidera exstinguere, Tartarum ipsum inluminare.
derivation: Direct-speech exchange: Aristomenes asks what kind of woman the innkeeper Meroe is; Socrates answers that she is a witch. Took the operative interrogative 'Potens illa et regina caupona quid mulieris est?' as the question (the preceding 'Ain tandem? inquam.' is a separate framing exclamation, omitted). The reply's framing tag 'inquit' is stripped; the answer runs verbatim and contiguous to its single full stop ('inluminare.'), which genuinely answers by characterizing her as 'Saga et divina'. What follows the cut is Lucius's next request, 'Oro te ... aulaeum tragicum dimoveto'.

question: Nostine Milonem quendam e primoribus?
answer: Vere primus istic perhibetur Milo, qui extra pomerium et urbem totam colit.
derivation: Direct-speech exchange: Lucius asks the old innkeeper woman whether she knows Milo, one of the leading men; she answers (with a pun on 'primoribus'/'primus') that Milo is reckoned foremost there and lives outside the whole city. Stripped the narration 'Adrisit et:' and the framing tag 'inquit'; normalized the initial capital. The answer runs verbatim and contiguous to its single full stop ('colit.'). What follows the cut is Lucius's next line, 'Remoto ioco, parens optima, dic oro et cuiatis sit'.

question: Meliora ominare et potius responde an intra aedes erum tuum offenderim.
answer: Plane.
derivation: Direct-speech exchange: Lucius asks the maid (indirect question 'an intra aedes erum tuum offenderim', whether he may find her master inside); she affirms 'Plane'. The question is Lucius's contiguous utterance verbatim (no framing narration to strip). The reply's framing tag 'inquit' is stripped and the answer is trimmed to its first word 'Plane.' (the affirmation); what follows the cut is the maid's own counter-question 'sed quae causa quaestionis huius?', which does not belong to the answer.

question: Quin etiam ipse parentem tuam accedis et salutas?
answer: Vereor ignotae mihi feminae.
derivation: The old man (senex) urges Lucius to greet the matron; Lucius declines. Dropped the framing 'inquit'. Answer is Lucius's full reply 'Vereor ignotae mihi feminae'; the following 'et statim rubore suffusus...' is narration, not utterance, so cut. Real interrogative answered by a declining response.

question: Qua corporis habitudine praeditus quove nomine nuncupatus hic iste Chaldaeus est?
answer: Procerus et suffusculus, Diophanes nomine.
derivation: Milo asks for the Chaldaean's appearance and name; Lucius answers with both. Dropped framing 'inquit' (Milo) and 'inquam' (Lucius). Answer is complete; what follows is Milo's next speech 'Ipse est ait...'.

question: Quam olim equidem exoptatus nobis advenis?
answer: Commodum vespera oriente.
derivation: Inside the Diophanes tale: Diophanes asks the young man how long ago he arrived; he answers 'Commodum vespera oriente'. Dropped the framing 'infit ad eum' / 'Respondit ad haec ille alius'. Cut before 'Sed vicissim tu quoque, frater...', where the speaker turns to a new request rather than answering.

question: Quam commode versaris in nostra patria?
answer: Vera memoras nec usquam gentium magis me liberum quam hic fuisse credidi.
derivation: Byrrhena asks Lucius how pleasantly he finds his stay (taking only her interrogative sentence; she then elaborates in praise of her city, which is her own speech, not the answer). Lucius's actual reply in 2.20 answers it. Dropped framing 'Ad haec ego subiciens'. Cut after the first full stop, before 'Sed oppido formido...', which digresses to fear of magic.

question: Quid hoc comperior? Hicine mortui solent aufugere?
answer: Tace, nam oppido puer et satis peregrinus es meritoque ignoras Thessaliae te consistere, ubi sagae mulieres ora mortuorum passim demorsicant, eaque sunt illis artis magicae supplementa.
derivation: Thelyphron, seeing a corpse-guard advertised, asks a passerby what is going on / whether the dead flee here; the passerby answers, explaining Thessalian witches. Dropped framing 'inquam' and 'respondit ille'. Answer runs to its full stop; this is the complete reply.

question: Et quae, tu, dic sodes, custodela ista feralis?
answer: Iam primum perpetem noctem eximie vigilandum est exsertis et inconivis oculis semper in cadaver intentis nec acies usquam devertenda, immo ne obliquanda quidem, quippe cum deterrimae versipelles in quodvis animal ore converso latenter adrepant, ut ipsos etiam oculos Solis et Iustitiae facile frustrentur; nam et aves et rursum canes et mures immo vero etiam muscas induunt.
derivation: Thelyphron asks what the funereal guard-duty consists of; the man answers, describing the vigil. Dropped framing 'inquam' and 'respondit ille'. Cut at the first full stop after 'muscas induunt'; the following 'Tunc diris cantaminibus somno custodes obruunt' begins further elaboration.

question: At quae ista sunt?
answer: Lucerna praegrandis et oleum ad lucem luci sufficiens et calida cum oenophoris et calice cenarumque reliquis discus ornatus.
derivation: Lucius asks for the necessities to be provided; the matron asks what those are ('At quae ista sunt?'), and Lucius lists them. Dropped framing 'inquit' and 'aio'. The referent of 'ista' is made explicit by the answering list. Answer is the complete enumeration; what follows is the matron's dismissive reply 'Abi fatue...'.

question: Quin refers populo singula tuaeque mortis illuminas arcana? An non putas devotionibus meis posse Diras invocari, posse tibi membra lassa torqueri?
answer: Malis novae nuptae peremptus artibus et addictus noxio poculo torum tepentem adultero mancipavi.
derivation: The Egyptian prophet, having revived the corpse, demands the dead youth reveal the secrets of his death; the youth answers that he was poisoned by his bride. Dropped framing 'ait' and 'Suscipit ille de lectulo et imo cum gemitu populum sic adorat'. Answer is the complete reply.

question: Sed, quod sciscitari praene praeterivi, quo dicto factove rursum exutis pinnulis illis ad meum redibo Lucium?
answer: Bono animo es, quod ad huius rei curam pertinet. Nam mihi domina singula monstravit, quae possunt rursus in facies hominum tales figuras reformare.
derivation: Lucius asks Photis by what word or deed he will, once the feathers are shed, return to being Lucius. Photis answers directly. Dropped the framing speech tag 'ait' that interrupts the reply. The answer window keeps the reassuring first sentence ('Bono animo es...') plus the operative answering sentence ('Nam mihi domina singula monstravit... reformare'), which states the means of reversal; cut before 'Nec istud factum putes ulla benivolentia...' where Photis turns to her motive and then to the specific herbal recipe, digressing from the asked question of by-what-means.

question: Etiamne tu, busti cadaver extremum et vitae dedecus primum et Orci fastidium solum, sic nobis otiosa domi residens lusitabis nec nostris tam magnis tamque periculosis laboribus solacium de tam sera refectione tribues?
answer: At vobis, fortissimi fidelissimeque mei sospitatores iuvenes, adfatim cuncta suavi sapore percocta pulmenta praesto sunt, panis numerosus vinum probe calicibus ecfricatis affluenter immissum et ex more calida tumultuario lavacro vestro praeparata.
derivation: The robbers interrogate the old woman with a real reproachful question ('Etiamne tu... lusitabis nec... solacium... tribues?'); I end the question at 'tribues?' and drop the following sentence 'Quae diebus ac noctibus...' which is a continuation of their taunt, not part of the interrogative. I drop the speech tags ('sic infesti compellant' before, 'sic anus' before her reply) and the framing 'Tremens ad haec et stridenti vocula pavida'. The answer is her operative reply asserting that all the food and bath are ready; it runs as one sentence to the full stop at 'praeparata.', then the narration 'In fine sermonis huius...' follows and is cut.

question: Quid, domina, tantis obstupescis opibus?
answer: Tua sunt haec omnia.
derivation: The disembodied voice addresses Psyche, asking and immediately answering itself. Stripped the speech tag 'inquit' (which interrupts the quotation: '"Quid," inquit "domina..."'). The question ends at its '?'; the answer is the next full sentence 'Tua sunt haec omnia.' The reply then digresses into commands ('Prohinc cubiculo te refer...'), so the window stops at the first full stop.

question: Quid vos miseris lamentationibus necquicquam effligitis?
answer: Quam lugetis, adsum.
derivation: Psyche calls out to her grieving sisters, asking why they wail, then answering that the one they mourn is present. Stripped the speech tag 'inquit' ('"Quid" inquit "vos..."'). The answer is the immediately following sentence; what follows ('Lugubres voces desinite...') turns to commands, so the window ends at the first full stop.

question: Ergo iam ille bonus filius meus habet amicam aliquam? Prome agedum, quae sola mihi servis amanter, nomen eius quae puerum ingenuum et investem sollicitavit, sive illa de Nympharum populo seu de Horarum numero seu de Musarum choro vel de mearum Gratiarum ministerio.
answer: Nescio, domina: puto puellam, si probe memini, Psyches nomine dici.
derivation: Venus asks the gull-bird for the name of her son's beloved; the bird answers with the name. The question is Venus's whole utterance (framing 'At Venus irata solidum exclamat repente:' precedes it and was dropped). For the answer, stripped the speech tag 'inquit' ('"Nescio," inquit "domina..."'); kept the contiguous reply through the name 'Psyches nomine dici', and cut the trailing clause 'illam dicitur efflicte cupere' which adds gossip beyond answering the name question.

question: Quid stas, Luci, vel quid iam novissimum exspectas?
answer: Mors et haec acerbissima decreto latronum tibi comparata est.
derivation: Lucius (as ass) addresses himself: 'et ipse mecum:' framing dropped. He poses the question and answers it himself in the very next sentence, telling himself what he is waiting for / why he stands still: death prepared by the robbers. Answer cut at the first full stop; what follows ('Nec magno conatu res indiget; vides istas rupinas...') turns from answering to elaborating on how to die, so it is excluded.

question: Quid miseros homines et laboriosos viatores tam crudelibus animis invaditis atque obteritis? Quas praedas inhiatis? Quae damna vindicatis? At non speluncas ferarum vel cautes incolitis barbarorum, ut humano sanguine profuso gaudeatis.
answer: At nos non vestrorum spoliorum cupidine latrocinamur, sed hanc ipsam cladem de vestris protelamus manibus.
derivation: The husband, under attack from dogs and stones, protests with a contiguous plea containing genuine interrogatives (Quid... invaditis? Quas praedas inhiatis? Quae damna vindicatis?); quoted entire and verbatim as the question. A villager from the cypress-top answers, explaining their motive. Dropped the framing 'inquit' (and the preceding 'Vnus illinc denique de summo cupressus cacumine:'). Answer ends at the first full stop ('...manibus.'); the following sentence 'Iam denique pace tranquilla securi potestis incedere.' is a follow-on reassurance, not part of the direct answer to why they attacked, so it is cut.

question: Adhucine miserum istum asinum iugi furore iactari credimus?
answer: Immo vero iam virus increscente saevitia prorsum extinctum.
derivation: Two of Lucius's guards debate ('altercare') whether the ass is still rabid. First speaker asks the interrogative ('Do we still think...?'); second answers 'Immo vero...' (no, the poison is now extinguished). Both verbatim quoted speech; no framing tags inside the quotes to strip.

question: Et quis est ille qui tanto praestinavit?
answer: Olim, inepte, descendit in dolium sedulo soliditatem eius probaturus.
derivation: Husband asks who bought the jar at such a price. Dropped the framing tag 'ait' between 'ille' and 'qui'. The wife's reply is introduced by framing 'At illa: ...inquit...' (dropped) and 'Olim, inepte' is her verbatim answer identifying the buyer as the man who 'long ago went down into the jar to test its soundness' (= the hidden adulterer). Answer ends at the full stop.

question: Ergo nostri totam Philesitheri et ipsius fabulam?
answer: Minime gentium, sed nosse valde cupio et oro, ordine mihi singula retexe.
derivation: The old bawd asks whether they know the whole story of Philesitherus. Dropped framing 'inquit anus' after 'Ergo'. The wife answers, framing tag 'inquit' (dropped) between 'gentium' and 'sed': 'By no means, but I greatly desire to know it; tell me each detail in order.' Genuine question and genuine answer; answer kept whole through the request as it is a single contiguous reply, not a digression.

question: Vnde autem tu, astutule asine, intra terminos pistrini contentus, quid secreto, ut adfirmas, mulieres gesserint scire potuisti?
answer: Accipe igitur quem ad modum homo curiosus iumenti faciem sustinens cuncta quae in perniciem pistoris mei gesta sunt cognovi.
derivation: The narrator anticipates the reader's objection and answers it himself. Dropped the framing introduction 'Sed forsitan lector scrupulosum reprehendes narratum meum sic argumentaberis:' before the quoted question. The answer 'Accipe igitur...' directly answers how he came to know the women's secret doings (as a curious man in a beast's shape). Answer ends at the first full stop, before the narrative resumes with 'Diem ferme circa mediam...'.

locus: De Ente et Essentia, cap. IV
question: Utrum ista natura sic considerata possit dici una vel plures?
answer: Neutrum concedendum est, quia utrumque est extra intellectum humanitatis et utrumque potest sibi accidere.
derivation: Authorial-rhetorical question and self-answer. Source: 'Unde si quaeratur utrum ista natura sic considerata possit dici una vel plures, neutrum concedendum est, quia utrumque est extra intellectum humanitatis et utrumque potest sibi accidere.' Dropped the asking-frame 'Unde si quaeratur' (narrates the posing of the question); capitalized 'Utrum' and added '?'. The answer runs from 'Neutrum' to the first full stop (the comma-joined causal clause is part of the same sentence); what follows ('Si enim pluralitas esset...') begins a new sentence elaborating the reasons, so it is cut. All other apparent interrogatives in the treatise are expository 'videndum est / restat videre / patet quod' statements, not posed-and-answered questions.

question: Regnum Dei semper fuit: quare ergo petimus quod veniat?
answer: Hoc potest tripliciter intelligi.
derivation: Dropped the framing 'Posset autem quaeri:' that narrates the posing of the question, and normalized the first word's capitalization. For the answer, dropped the framing opener 'Et ideo dicendum est, quod' leaving the operative response 'Hoc potest tripliciter intelligi' (cut at the first full stop); what follows is the threefold exposition 'Primo quia aliquando rex habet ius regni...'.

question: Si omnia facit quae vult in caelo et in terra, quid est hoc quod dicit: fiat voluntas tua sicut in caelo, et in terra?
answer: Deus tria vult de nobis, et nos petimus quod haec impleantur.
derivation: The interrogative span is the author's own self-posed question. For the answer, dropped the framing opener 'Ad hoc sciendum est, quod' leaving 'Deus tria vult de nobis, et nos petimus quod haec impleantur' (cut at the first full stop); what follows enumerates the three things ('Primum quidem quod Deus vult de nobis...').

question: Ex quo dimittitur peccatum contritione, ad quid necessarius est sacerdos?
answer: Deus in contritione dimittit culpam, et poena aeterna commutatur in temporalem; sed nihilominus manet adhuc obligatus ad poenam temporalem.
derivation: Dropped the framing 'Sed forte quis dicet:' that narrates the objection being raised, and normalized capitalization. For the answer, dropped the framing opener 'Ad hoc dicendum est, quod' leaving the operative reply (cut at the first full stop); what follows elaborates the role of the priest ('Unde si decederet sine confessione... iret ad Purgatorium').

question: Utrum ille qui non proponit dimittere proximo suo, debeat dicere: sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris?
answer: Non mentitur, quia non orat in persona sua, sed Ecclesiae, quae non decipitur.
derivation: Dropped the framing 'Sed quaeritur' that narrates the question being raised, normalized capitalization, and put a terminal question mark on the indirect-question clause. The scholastic 'Videtur quod non, quia mentitur' is omitted as it is the objection, not the question. For the answer, dropped the framing opener 'Dicendum, quod' leaving 'Non mentitur, quia non orat in persona sua, sed Ecclesiae, quae non decipitur' (cut at the first full stop); what follows is the corollary 'et ideo ponitur ipsa petitio in plurali'.

question: Ergo Christum decipere quaeris?
answer: Sed certe non decipis.
derivation: Author's rhetorical question to the reader, directly answered by the next sentence. Kept the contiguous answer to its full stop; what follows ('Nam Christus qui hanc orationem fecit, bene recordatur eius') explains why.

question: Sed nunquid Deus inducit ad malum, quia dicit: et ne nos inducas in tentationem?
answer: Deus dicitur inducere ad malum permittendo, inquantum scilicet propter multa peccata subtrahit homini gratiam suam, qua sublata homo labitur in peccatum.
derivation: Author's self-posed question (nunquid). For the answer, dropped the framing opener 'Dico, quod' leaving the operative reply (cut at the first full stop); what follows is a Psalm citation 'et ideo cantamus in Psalmo LXX, 9...'.

locus: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q.10 a.2
question: Utrum Deus sit aeternus?
answer: Unde, cum Deus sit maxime immutabilis, sibi maxime competit esse aeternum.
derivation: Question is the article-2 Utrum title (a real interrogative), answered by Aquinas in the Respondeo. The Respondeo opens with a non-answering general principle ('ratio aeternitatis consequitur immutabilitatem, sicut ratio temporis consequitur motum, ut ex dictis patet.'), so the answer start is advanced to the operative answering sentence beginning 'Unde, cum Deus...'. Cut at the first full stop; what follows ('Nec solum est aeternus, sed est sua aeternitas...') elaborates and is omitted.

locus: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q.10 a.3
question: Utrum esse aeternum sit proprium Dei?
answer: Aeternitas vere et proprie in solo Deo est.
derivation: Question is the article-3 Utrum title, answered by Aquinas in the Respondeo. The first sentence of the Respondeo ('Respondeo dicendum quod aeternitas vere et proprie in solo Deo est.') directly and fully answers; framing 'Respondeo dicendum quod' is dropped as narration of the response and the first word capitalized. Cut at the first full stop; what follows ('Quia aeternitas immutabilitatem consequitur...') gives the supporting reasons and is omitted.

locus: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q.10 a.4
question: Utrum aeternitas differat a tempore?
answer: Manifestum est tempus et aeternitatem non esse idem.
derivation: Question is the article-4 Utrum title, answered by Aquinas in the Respondeo. The first sentence of the Respondeo ('Respondeo dicendum quod manifestum est tempus et aeternitatem non esse idem.') directly answers (time and eternity are not the same, i.e. eternity does differ from time); framing 'Respondeo dicendum quod' dropped and first word capitalized. Cut at the first full stop; what follows ('Sed huius diversitatis rationem quidam assignaverunt...') discusses the basis of the difference and is omitted.

locus: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q.10 a.6
question: Utrum sit unum aevum tantum?
answer: Et quia secunda opinio verior est, ut infra ostendetur, concedimus ad presens unum esse aevum tantum.
derivation: Question is the article-6 Utrum title, answered by Aquinas's concluding determination in the Respondeo. The Respondeo opens by laying out two opinions ('circa hoc est duplex opinio...') and argues at length without answering, so the answer start is advanced to Aquinas's operative determination, the final contiguous sentence 'Et quia secunda opinio verior est... concedimus ad presens unum esse aevum tantum.' (there is one aeviternity only). This is a single contiguous sentence, not stitched; the long intervening argument is omitted.

locus: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I q.11 a.1
question: Utrum unum addat aliquid supra ens?

question: Numquid ergo illa quae restant non sunt ventura?
answer: Manifestum est quia sicut ista praedicta venerunt, sic etiam illa ventura sunt, quaecumque tribulationes justorum adhuc restant, et judicii dies, qui separabit omnes impios a justis in resurrectione mortuorum, et non solum eos qui sunt extra Ecclesiam, sed etiam ipsius Ecclesiae paleas, quas oportet usque ad novissimam ventilationem patientissime sufferat, ad ignem debitum segregabit.
